description: Global fire monitoring faces a critical obstacle: the historical incompatibility between MODIS and VIIRS satellite data. Harmonizing these records is essential to build a continuous history that allows anticipating fire patterns, assessing risk areas, and aiding in emergencies. Our skills converge in solving this issue. We bring a solid analytical vision for complex systems modeling, logical algorithm formulation, and data analysis, deeply understanding how thermal anomalies impact ecosystems.
summary: The Hexatech team developed an accessible web-based solution that transforms nearly 25 years of fragmented observations (2002–2026) into a continuous, comparable, and transparent interactive calendar, bringing the entire historical record to the resolution scale of VIIRS. The challenge is addressed by dividing the territory into a grid of 5 km × 5 km (0.05°) cells to measure activity in active cell-days—avoiding the overcounting that occurs when a higher-resolution sensor records the same fire across multiple pixels—and training an algorithm that learns how many VIIRS cell-days correspond to MODIS according to geographic block, month, and heat power, focused on the Argentine Dry Chaco. Its importance lies in preventing the loss of more than a decade of historical information ahead of MODIS’s imminent retirement and demonstrating that the apparent increase in fires in 2012 was a technological jump, revealing that an estimated 67% more fire activity and nearly twice as many annual hotspots could be identified during the 2003–2011 period than in the following decade. In addition, it achieves blind-test accuracy with only a 7.1% error in activity and 7.8% in hotspots, enabling the identification of real anomalies without allowing the technology to distort history.
details:
The HEXA Harmonization Model, developed by the Hexatech team, is an algorithmic solution and interactive web platform that converts nearly 25 years of satellite thermal records (from 2002 to 2026) in the Argentine Dry Chaco into a single continuous, comparable, and transparent calendar expressed at the high-resolution scale of the VIIRS S-NPP sensor (375 m). 

The project was developed in Python 3.9+ using libraries such as pandas and numpy to process NASA FIRMS data and ecoregion vector layers, generating reproducible scripts (armonizar_desde_crudo.py, construir_modelo_unificado.py) and standardized data files (.csv) that feed the web interface. Among its main benefits and expected impact, the tool prevents the loss of more than a decade of historical records ahead of the imminent retirement of the MODIS sensor and eliminates the distortion caused by the 2012 technological jump, demonstrating—with a blind-tested monthly error of 6.5% to 7.8% —that an estimated 67% more fire activity and 1.92 times more annual hotspots could be identified during the 2003–2011 period than in the following decade, providing researchers and environmental managers with a truthful and transparent input for territorial decision-making.ncc.nesdis.noaa+6 

To address the challenge, the system divides the territory into 17,916 cells of 5 km (0.05°), grouped into 64 blocks of 1°, and independently processes three dimensions: activity in cell-days, hotspot counts, and fire radiative power (FRP in MW). During the period when both sensors overlapped (2013–2025), the model trains decision trees with 23 variables derived from MODIS to estimate activity by block and month, applies independent conversion factors for daytime and nighttime passes when counting hotspots , and translates intensity quantile by quantile by grouping detections into events . It also distributes monthly activity across days using a saturation function with an exponent of 0.6 .ncc.nesdis.noaa+1 

This methodology stands out for its creativity in rejecting fixed global factors and direct sensor sums, instead isolating VIIRS’s greater nighttime sensitivity, measuring activity in cell-days to mitigate spatial overcounting, and preserving the actual shape of the fire radiative power distribution without inflating low-activity days. To ensure maximum robustness, the Hexatech team considered key factors such as the climate variability of the Dry Chaco, geographic heterogeneity by block , strict detection of days with sensor outages (Rule 0) to avoid assuming false zeros , the orbital drift of the Aqua satellite from 2023 onward , and rigorous out-of-sample (“blind”) validation that evaluates error only on years not seen during model fitting .
